The spec is unusually complete — no `[NEEDS CLARIFICATION]` markers, 37 requirements, 8 measurable criteria, and an Assumptions section that deliberately closes several open details. My scan found four genuinely unresolved areas that would change implementation and test design, so I'll work through them one at a time.

---

**Question:** When the service encounters a stored snippet whose file it cannot read or parse — truncated by a crash, hand-edited, or written by an incompatible version — what should it do?

**Why it matters:** The spec guarantees no unhandled failures for every input it describes (FR-037), but a damaged file on disk isn't an "input", so today there's no defined behaviour — and the difference between answering "not found" and raising a loud error decides whether silent data loss can go unnoticed.

**Recommended:** Option B — Constitution Principle II ("Fail Loudly", and specifically its ban on returning a value a caller could mistake for a result) means a corrupt snippet must not masquerade as a deleted one; reporting it loudly while leaving other snippets served also avoids a startup scan that would work against the 2-second readiness target in SC-007.

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| A | Treat the snippet as not found (404), write a warning to the error stream, keep serving everything else |
| B | Report an internal error (500) with an explanatory error body for that snippet only, write a diagnostic to the error stream, keep serving everything else |
| C | Refuse to start at all if any stored snippet is unreadable, reporting it and exiting non-zero |
| D | Leave it unspecified — out of scope for this feature, record as an assumption |
| Short | Provide a different short answer (<=5 words) |

You can reply with the option letter (e.g., "A"), accept the recommendation by saying "yes" or "recommended", or provide your own short answer.
